en: *Hetuvidyānyāyamukha-śāstra*, one fascicle.
Composed by Bodhisattva Śubhagupta;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The Commentary says:
Desiring to distinguish and uphold the reality within the meanings of proof and refutation, this treatise is composed.
The Verse says:
The thesis (*pakṣa*) and other such verbal expressions constitute the proof (*sādhana*);
therein, it is solely according to one's own intention that what is intended to be established is called the "thesis," and not that which contradicts its meaning which could refute it.
The treatise states:
This treatise is now composed to establish the meaning of the proof (*sādhana*) and to seal the meaning of reality (*tattva*).
The statement that "the thesis and other factors constitute the proof," and so forth, is intended to clarify the introduction, the subject matter (*abhidheya*), and the purpose (*prayojana*).
Regarding the "introduction" (*nidāna*), it refers to the causal conditions consisting of the benefit of all sentient beings and so forth.
Regarding the "expressed meaning" (*abhidheya*), it refers to the meanings expressed, namely the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so on.
The purpose for which this treatise is composed is to establish the definitive meaning.

If it were intended merely to manifest the causal origins and so forth, then placing these words at the beginning of this treatise would be redundant, as this meaning has already been manifested elsewhere—just as in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). What, then, is meant by "manifested elsewhere"?
Because it would be improper to state [the reason] at the beginning when it is already explained at the end of the treatise.
If that were so, then because it is not a constituent part of the treatise, it would be like any other extraneous statement.
However, since this meaning has already been clarified elsewhere, this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Regarding the phrase "understanding the meaning only at a later time after the treatise has been explained": through the wisdom of awakening, one first hears the introductory context and so forth; if one does not comprehend it initially, the [realization] does not arise. It is only by virtue of this subsequent understanding that one accords with the truth at a later time.
Because it does not constitute a section of the treatise, this [claim] is also untenable.
Even if such were the intention, since it is neither a sūtra nor a commentary on one, it certainly cannot be a constituent part; who then would explain this sūtra?
Who has ever explained this?

Therefore, one should know that just as Devadatta’s speech does not constitute a constituent part [of the argument], the introductory passages of various treatises do indeed constitute such parts; since this reason exists, the charge of being unestablished (*asiddha*) is avoided.
Another further objects, saying:
"Do not compose this treatise, for it lacks a logical basis (*yukti*) and so forth, being like the words of a madman.
This is to demonstrate that the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Answer: It refers to that which is capable of establishing [a position], capable of refuting [an opponent], and so forth.
If one says this, do not compose such a treatise, because the meaning has already been revealed through the description itself, as in the second *Nyāyamukha*.
Akṣapāda has already explained the characteristics of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, because his words indicate that [the opponent's position] is not established.
Is it not the case that the *sādhana* (means of proof) and other factors must be marked by the reality of their meaning?
However, since this treatise and others do not mark the meaning as real, there is the fault of non-establishment (*asiddha*).
The preceding section has already analyzed the proponent’s presentation of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Below, the main text shall be explained in successive order.

Regarding the statement, "A collection of multiple statements, such as the thesis and so forth, constitutes the proof" (*sādhanam*): because one elucidates for others meanings not yet understood through the verbal exposition of multiple statements—namely, the thesis, the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—this collection of multiple statements is termed "proof" (*sādhana*) in works such as the *Vādanyāya*.

Furthermore, the statement that "a single member [of the proof] is sufficient to establish [the thesis]" is intended to demonstrate that the nature of being a complete proof is established as a whole; from this, it should be understood that the failure of any one of these members constitutes a fault of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*).
The term "in this" (*asmin*) signifies the commencement of the treatise, or the sense of selection and retention; it is called "in this" because it refers to the thesis and so forth.
The term "only" (*eva*) has the sense of exclusion.
"Following one's own intention" (svatantra) indicates that one disregards the tenets of other treatises and establishes [the position] according to one's own intention.
"Desire" (ruci) is what is to be established; that is, the absence of desire is the nature of the means of establishment.
If it were otherwise, then the "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*) and the "pseudo-example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), which are what are being established, would also have to be called the "thesis" (*pakṣa*).
To clarify that the thesis is distinct from these other faults, it is said: "It cannot be set aside by a meaning that contradicts it."
If it is not set aside by a statement that contradicts its own meaning— such as the proposition "all statements are false"— or if it contradicts the previously established tenet,
such as the son of a Hūṇa (Vaiśeṣika) establishing "sound is eternal"; or if, because it is a unique [reason], there is no inference available,

and it is set aside by a contradiction with a universally accepted statement, such as saying "the hare-holder is not the moon, because it exists" [when it is universally accepted that the hare-holder *is* the moon].

Furthermore, regarding an existent phenomenon, there is the refutation of a meaning that contradicts what is established by that very [proponent] through the consensus of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), such as when one attempts to establish that "sound is not audible" or that "a jar is permanent."

Regarding those who claim that when the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) contradict each other, it is called a "contradiction of the thesis" (*pakṣavirodha*), this is not a fault of the thesis;

for in this case, the formulation "Sound is permanent, because everything is impermanent" is an instance of a poorly established dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) used as a rhetorical device, which, by means of the application (*upanaya*), demonstrates that [the subject] is not included among "everything."
This reason does not exist, because sound is included within "all" [things].
Alternatively, because it is a part of the very meaning of the thesis (*sādhya*), this argument fails; thus, it is termed a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
The analogy is also flawed, because it first demonstrates the absence of the thesis through a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), and only subsequently states the absence of the reason.
It should have been stated thus:
"All things are impermanent" means that it is not the case that "they are not all [eternal]."
However, since this inverted statement claims that "all things are impermanent," the analogy used herein is also flawed.
Thus, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the fallacious thesis have been explained.
Since the reason (*hetu*) and the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are for the most part properties of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), their specific characteristics shall now be demonstrated.
The verse says:
Regarding the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) in similar instances (sapakṣa), it is said to be present, absent, or both;
in dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), there are likewise three possibilities: present, absent, or both.
The treatise says:
Is it not the case that the thesis (*pakṣa*) is defined as the synthesis of the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) with the locus (*dharmin*)?
Why, then, is it said here that the thesis refers only to the locus?
There is no fault here,
because a general term may also apply to its specific instances, as in the expression "burning the robe"; or,
in some schools, the term *dharma* refers exclusively to phenomena.
In this context, the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) is taken only as that which is definitively accepted by both the proponent and the opponent.
The same applies to its presence or absence within the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Why is this? Because here it relies solely on the cause of realization (*pratyaya-hetu*); one understands the meaning of what is taught through the power of wisdom alone, rather than like a generative cause (*janaka-hetu*) which functions by producing an effect.
If that were so, since cognition (*jñāna*) is taken as the instrumental cause (*paricchedaka-hetu*), this statement would lose its capacity to establish [the probandum].

This is not the case, however, because it causes one to recollect what was originally established. Therefore, in this context, taking only that which is admitted by both parties as certain constitutes a sound explanation.

Therefore, if there is a disagreement between the proponent and the opponent regarding a particular point, it certainly cannot be considered a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); for example, as in the attempt to prove that "sound is impermanent because it is visible to the eye."
Furthermore, if the opponent does not grant the same admission, it is like the case of the *Prasanga-vādin* [opposing] with "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).

Or, if there is doubt, as when one gives rise to uncertainty based on smoke and so forth, one establishes: "There is fire resulting from the combination of the primary elements (*mahābhūta-saṃyoga*), because smoke is presently perceived."
Alternatively, in some instances, a thesis is not established, such as when one attempts to prove that "the self is omnipresent because pleasure and so forth arise in all locations.
All such statements of every kind mentioned above are incapable of establishing a proof.
The same should be stated accordingly regarding their presence or absence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and so forth.

Among the reasons that will be explained as contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), only those expressed with words whose certainty is universally acknowledged are designated as "proof" (*sādhana*) or "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*).
This is not a case of mutual non-establishment or of words expressing doubt, for it must further depend upon establishment.
Now, when establishing a thesis-property (*pakṣadharma*), it is logically necessary to establish this property by means of another property as a reason (*hetu*):

whether one establishes that the subject (*dharmin*) exists, or establishes it as non-existent—for example, as when one establishes "The Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) exists, because we perceive distinct individual things belonging to a common class."
Alternatively, it may be established as "non-existent, because it cannot be apprehended.
What is the meaning of this?
Here, one merely establishes the thesis that "a distinct entity necessarily possesses a single cause," rather than establishing "supremacy"; therefore, this fault does not apply.

If it is established as "non-existent," one nevertheless provisionally designates it as a "dharma that cannot be apprehended"; therefore, there is likewise no fault of [falling into] the existence of a dharma.

If one were to establish another existent dharma by means of an existent dharma, or establish its own nature—for example, establishing fire by means of smoke, or establishing tangibility by means of fire—what would the meaning of this be?
In this context, it is not the case that "fire" and "touch" are established as the thesis (*pakṣa*); rather, it is the object associated with them that is being established.
Otherwise, if fire were established based on smoke and touch were established based on fire, it would follow that a portion of the thesis itself constitutes the reason (*hetu*).
Furthermore, in this context, it is not intended to establish the existence of fire or touch, as their existence is already commonly known.

Moreover, since one examines the probandum (sādhya) within this context, one posits the property (dharma) and the property-bearer (dharmin), rather than the attribute (guṇa) and the possessor of attributes (guṇin); therefore, there is no fault.
Repeating this in verse:
There is a phenomenon that does not establish a phenomenon, nor does a phenomenon establish this [other] phenomenon;
only by means of a phenomenon is that phenomenon established— in this way is a phenomenon established.
The treatise says:

If one establishes the thesis that "sound is not eternal because karma and so forth must be eternal, and because what is eternal should be perceptible," how is this termed a *pakṣadharma* (property of the subject)?

This explains the opponent's fault by means of the "reason" (*hetu*) and "thesis" (*pakṣa*) sections; because the word "should" (*syāt*) is employed when there is something to be established, one first establishes [the reason] as "it is permanent, because it is formless," and subsequently establishes only the thesis to refute the fault of that reason.
If one establishes the proposition in this way: "Sound is impermanent, because that which is produced is not eternal, and that which is eternal is not produced," how is this further characterized?
It is a skillful means of illustration.

The similar instance (*sādharmya*) and the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*) proclaim their respective reasons in due order, because the thesis (*pakṣa*) necessarily follows them, and because where there is no thesis, there is necessarily no reason.

In this context, by means of the application (*upanaya*), the reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is demonstrated: thus, this sound is necessarily produced and not unproduced; this quality of being produced is necessarily a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Re-stated in verse:
When the reason is stated, it follows the thesis;
when the thesis is absent, the reason does not exist.
Based on the fifth [verse], the illustration is revealed; through conjunction, the reason is known.
The treatise says:

By this, the method of refutation by reversal has already been explained. Because "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is observed in the impermanent and not observed in the permanent, it is thus established that "sound is not permanent, because it would not be produced."
Therefore, the methods of conforming and establishing [a position] or opposing and refuting it are not separate reasons for understanding.
As I have already extensively analyzed in the refutation of the Sāṃkhya school, I shall now cease this extensive debate on these ancillary arguments.
Thus, there are three distinctions in the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), namely:
presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), absence from it, and both.
First, exclude the word "and" (*ca*).
In this context, if a category is proximate and equivalent to the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*), it is called the "similar class" (*sapakṣa*), because all objects are termed "classes.
If the property to be established is absent, it is called the "dissimilar class" (*vipakṣa*); this does not mean it is either contradictory to or different from the similar class.
If they were contradictory, there would need to be a specific distinction made;
if they were different, there would be no cause [for their coexistence].
By this principle, "the state of being produced" can establish both "impermanence" and "selflessness," because they are not contradictory.
If a property can establish a contradictory thesis, it is a contradictory fallacy (*viruddha-doṣa*), which is termed a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*).
Just as with the non-contradictory (*aviruddha*), so too is the contradictory:
because when the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is absent, [the reason] is necessarily absent.
It is not like the case of a jar and such, where doubt arises because an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not exist between them;

for while the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is clearly observed to exist in cloth and so forth apart from a jar, this reason does not exist apart from impermanence (*anityatva*) in things such as the selfless (*anātman*).
How can a distinct phenomenon (*dharma*) function in a distinct location?
Because they are similar, it is not stated by a different name; rather, it is said that "this is precisely that," and thus there is no fault.
If it is not stated as something distinct, how can this reason be called the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*)?
In this context, it is stated that [the reason] must necessarily be a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), but it is not intended to say that it is *only* a property of the thesis.
If that were the case, would the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) also be called the thesis? No;
for it is stated elsewhere that the similar instance is that which is to be established (*sādhya*).
The reason must be without exception for an inference (*anumāna*) to be established; therefore, it is not [merely] similar.

Furthermore, each of these has three types: namely, that which exists in all similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and regarding its dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), it may exist, not exist, or both exist and not exist.
Regarding their absence from the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and their presence in both [the similar and dissimilar classes], each has these three types of distinctions.

If the thesis of impermanence has no dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) at all—such as when debating against those who do not posit the existence of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth—how can one say that this [reason] is absent in that place?
If that [reason] does not exist [in the subject], it does not occur therein; since there is no doubt whatsoever [regarding its absence], this fault does not arise.

Thus, nine types of thesis-reasons (*pakṣadharma*) are formed in total. To briefly explain their characteristics in their respective order: one might establish "Sound is eternal, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*)," or establish "It is impermanent, because it is produced (*kṛtakatva*)."
Some may establish [the thesis] as "it is impermanent because it is produced by effort without interval";
some may establish it as "it is permanent because it is a product";
or some may establish it as "it is permanent because it is audible."
Some establish [the subject] as "permanent," because it is produced by constant and uninterrupted effort;
some [establish it] as "not produced by constant and uninterrupted effort," because it is impermanent;
and some establish it as "impermanent," because it is produced by constant and uninterrupted effort.
Or it is established as "permanent, because it is not subject to contact.
These nine types are subsumed within two verses, which state:
Permanence, impermanence, and exertion; constancy, abiding, and the nature of solidity;
non-exertion, transition, and immutability—these are established by the nine [reasons], beginning with "being an object of cognition."
The object of cognition, activity, impermanence; the nature of activity, hearing, and the arousal of valor;
impermanence, valor, and lack of contact—these nine, beginning with permanence, are the bases.
The Commentary says:
Such distinctions are termed "the reason" (*hetu*), "contradictory" (*viruddha*), and "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, the root verse states:
"In that which exists in the similar class and both [classes], And is absent in the dissimilar class, this is the reason."
The opposite of this is called "contradictory" (*viruddha*); all others are "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
Among these, there are only two types of reasons (*hetu*): namely, that which exists throughout the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and is entirely absent from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*);
and that which exists in some but not all of the similar instances and is entirely absent from the dissimilar instances.
From the first and last [of each group], one takes the middle one from each.

Furthermore, only two types are said to be contradictory because they establish perversion: namely, that which exists in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) and both types [existence and non-existence];
whereas it is entirely absent from all similar instances (sapakṣa).
Among the second triad, one takes the first and the last two.
The remaining five types are non-definitive in terms of both their causes and their contradictions; this is the meaning of being a "cause of doubt.

Furthermore, regarding all characteristics of reasons (*hetu*) and so forth, it is stated that the subject and its predicate share the same number and class. This is to ensure that two contradictory characteristics are not described as coalescing in a single place while still functioning as a reason, or that a single characteristic does not become a non-pervasive reason (*avyāpaka-hetu*) because it performs the same function [as another].

Logically, all four types should be called "inconclusive reasons" (*anaikāntika-hetu*), because both [the presence of the reason in the subject and its absence from the dissimilar instances] apply to them.
What is meant by "that which is heard"?
It is so called because it is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
Because those specific differences among the properties to be established that are not shared [with the dissimilar class] encompass all such cases, they are all reasons for doubt;
for they are exclusively excluded from that which possesses the property [of the similar class].
All that exists is common [to all], for there is no cause for distinction.
This alone is not mutually contradictory with respect to them; it is the nature of a cause for doubt.
If, within this, both parts are present, it is also a definitive cause because it distinguishes [it] from others; this is called "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*).
If one were to concede that the nature of sound is eternal, this [reason] would indeed be a valid probans (*sādhana*).
If, at that time, there were no manifestation of such factors as being produced (*kṛtaka*) as reasons for impermanence, this interpretation might be possible;
however, since both [the reason and its opposite] are apprehended simultaneously and their meanings are contradictory, they cannot coexist, and thus it is a reason of doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*).
Furthermore, within this context, the power of direct manifestation and scriptural teaching is superior; therefore, one should rely upon these to seek certainty.
A summary verse states:
"If a phenomenon is unique, common, or characterized by definitive contradiction,"
In all cases regarding those [objects], these are all of the nature of causes for doubt. Whether it be a false proof (*asiddha*),
the existence of a property (*dharmasattva*), its essential nature (*svabhāva*), or its specific distinction (*viśeṣa*),
these constitute contradictory reasons (*viruddhahetu*) if they are not sublated by what is contrary to them.

When examining the fundamental tenets of a school through critical investigation, if what is cherished is contradicted or harmed, one falls into hesitation and cognitive inversion; apart from this, there is no similar cause.
The treatise says:
Having thus already analyzed the reasons (*hetu*) and pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*),
I shall now explain the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) and pseudo-examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
The verse says:
It is said that the reason follows the thesis;
if the thesis is absent, the reason does not exist.
These two are called analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*); all others are similar to these.
The treatise states:
There are two kinds of analogies:
those based on similarity (sādharmya) and those based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya).
A "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) refers to establishing: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced by continuous effort.
For all things produced by continuous effort are seen to be impermanent, just like a jar and so forth."
The "dissimilar property" (*vaidharmya*) refers to the statement: "Whatever is eternal is not produced by uninterrupted effort, such as space and so forth.

The former [the similar property] is both a negation and an affirmation, while the latter merely serves to exclude over-extension; this is because they function through the logical inference of conjunction and disjunction.

Consequently, although one does not establish the actual existence of such things as "great empty space" (*mahākāśa*) through formal debate, it is nonetheless possible to demonstrate that the thesis (*pakṣa*) does not exist and that the meaning of the absence of a reason (*hetu*) is established.

Furthermore, for what reason is it stated in the first [case] that the reason follows upon the thesis, while in the second it is stated that the thesis does not exist because the reason is absent, rather than stating that the thesis does not exist because the reason is absent?

By stating it in this way, one demonstrates that the reason is necessarily present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and entirely absent in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), rather than stating it erroneously.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"One should prove its permanence by means of its non-productivity, Or establish its productivity by means of its impermanence."
If that were so, it would result in what was not stated: namely, that [the self] is neither pervasive, nor conjoined with pleasure and so forth, nor dissociated from them.
The treatise says:
Thus have the two sets of analogies for the conjunction and dissociation of the two factors—both the concordant and the counter-examples—already been explained.
The "remainder" that is similar to this constitutes the meaning of a "pseudo-example.
What is meant by "this remainder"?

It refers to cases where, regarding the thesis (*sādhya*), the proof (*sādhana*), and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), although there is a combination or separation [of these elements], they are stated in a perverted manner.

Alternatively, in this case, there is no application or exclusion; rather, only the presence of both the *sādhya* (the probandum) and the *sādhana* (the probans) is established, while both are absent from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
Regarding these two properties, it may be that either one is unestablished or not excluded, or it may be that both are unestablished and not excluded.
For example, one might establish the thesis: "Sound is eternal, because it lacks tangibility.
As a supporting illustration based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one might say: "Whatever lacks tangibility is seen to be eternal, such as karma, atoms, or a jar," and so forth.

Regarding the statement of a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), it refers to such claims as: "All impermanent things are observed to possess tangibility, like atoms, like karma, or like space.

By this, it has already been explained that there is a failure to establish the subject (*dharmin*) within a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), namely, when one opposes those who do not admit that space and so forth are permanent.
Must both types of analogical expressions be provided for the proof (sādhana) to be established?
Or may it be as with the reason (*hetu*), where only one is stated?

According to correct reasoning, both should be stated; for by providing both, one fully demonstrates that the probandum (*sādhya*) is not separate from its reason, thereby fully showing its necessary presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its total absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), which correctly counteracts the fallacies of contradiction (*viruddha*) and uncertainty (*anaikāntika*).
If one part [of the reason] is already established for [the opponent], stating that same part also constitutes a valid proof (*sādhana*).
If, as in the case of the word "sound," both parties agree upon both meanings, there is no need to state either of them.
Alternatively, by implication, one [mark] can manifest two [conclusions].
Furthermore, this principle is observed solely within inference (*anumāna*):

if this mark is ascertained at the locus of inference, one recalls its definite presence in other similar instances and its universal absence in those where it is absent; thus, from this, a definitive understanding arises.
Therefore, the root verse says:
"Just as one has attained certainty for oneself, One desires that others attain certainty;
thus, one states The thesis, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), and the logical connection (*sambandha*), While remaining free from all else."
The Commentary states:
The term "reason" (hetu) is spoken in order to manifest the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) within that which is to be inferred;
the term "example" (dṛṣṭānta) is spoken in order to manifest the inseparable relationship (avinābhāvitva) therein.
The thesis (pakṣa) is stated in order to manifest that which is to be inferred (anumeya).

Within that which is to be inferred, there are no other constituent members besides this; therefore, it excludes other elements such as examination (parīkṣā), as well as the application (upanaya) and the conclusion (nigamana).
If that were the case, the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would not be a distinct member [of the syllogism], because it would merely manifest the meaning of the reason (*hetu*).

Although this is indeed the case, the statement of the reason is intended solely to manifest its status as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*); it does not manifest the presence or absence [of the reason] in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, the statements of the similar and dissimilar examples must be stated separately.
If the meaning expressed by the words "reason" (*hetu*) alone is what is called the "reason," what fault would there be?
And what benefit would there be?
To state the section on the "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) separately is the benefit.
This should be understood as being entirely inconsistent with the meaning of the "reason" (*hetu*) according to the worldly conventions of "expedient means" (*upāya*).
If this were so, what would be the fault?

This statement merely serves as an illustration of the point to be established—that [the reason] lacks functional capacity and is not a valid "prover" (*sādhana*), because it merely states the property of being "produced" (*kṛtakatva*), which is the common property shared with the subject.
It does not state the meaning of the probans (*sādhana*) or the probandum (*sādhya*).

Furthermore, because the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are distinct, this [reason] possesses both the similar instance (*sādharmya*) and the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*), yet it ultimately cannot manifest the inseparability (*avinābhāva*) between the reason and the probandum. Therefore, while it merely resembles the meaning of the probandum, it lacks functional efficacy.
Why is it incapable? Because within a homologous example (*sapakṣa*), the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣārtha*) do not necessarily correspond;
furthermore, since this would have to be established by yet another example, it would lead to an infinite regress.

Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that there are various categories; nor can something from a different category—which does not manifest the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) and lacks any distinguishing qualification—serve as an analogy.
Thus, a verse says:
"If the reason is merely the thesis itself, Or if it belongs to a different class of characteristics,"
The analogies would be endless, as well as the exclusion of dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
The treatise states:

In the world, one merely employs a "dissimilar example" (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) to demonstrate that the reason (*hetu*) exists in the same location as the dissimilar instances of the thesis (*pakṣa*); it is not because the reason lacks existence in places where the thesis is absent that its capacity is definitively negated.
If the mere property of the subject were the nature of the reason, then even that which is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) would necessarily become a valid reason.

How could such a fallacy occur when both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), as well as the two types of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*)—namely, those of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)—are fully present?

If, at that time, the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) established were of more than one type, this fault would indeed arise; however, as in the case of the first and last three [reasons] where each has its own final example, the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) are definitively intended solely to reveal the logical reason (*hetu*).
By this principle, although every component is capable of serving as a reason to manifest the thesis (*sādhya*), only one component is stated for the time being as the reason.

Thus, the brief exposition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, along with their fallacious counterparts (*ābhāsa*), constitutes what is called the "proof" (*sādhana*) and its "fallacious counterpart."
According to what is appropriate for others, these means of proof (*sādhana*) and fallacious means of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) are taught for the sake of their enlightenment.

For one's own enlightenment, however, there are only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); since terms such as "sound" and "example" are subsumed within these two, there are only two means of valid cognition.

Because it is through this that one can discern both specifically characterized (*svalakṣaṇa*) and generally characterized (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) objects, there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) apart from these two for which another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be established.
Therefore, the root verse says:
"Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); The others are said to arise from causes."
The treatise states:

Regarding the phrase "direct perception excludes conceptualization" (*pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍham*), this means that if there is a cognition which, with respect to objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, is free from all types of conceptualization—including those involving names, designations, conventional constructs, non-differentiation, and various categories—and which functions individually and manifestly based on its own specific conditions, it is therefore called direct perception.
Therefore, it is said in verse:
The dharmas do not have a single characteristic; The faculties do not encompass all modes of activity.
Only through internal realization and beyond words Is the realm of the physical faculties known.
The Commentary states:
Within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), there is also that which functions as direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) apart from all conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, the self-cognizing portions (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*) of craving and so forth, as well as the states of those practicing meditative concentration who are free from conceptualization based on scripture, are all forms of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, within this [self-cognition], there is no separate result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), because this very essence arises as if it were an object and appears as if it had utility; thus, it is metaphorically designated as "valid cognition.
If self-cognition regarding desire and so forth is also direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), why is conceptual cognition excluded from this category?
This does not exclude self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) within this context, for it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
However, that which, within this [self-cognition], cognizes other objects is not termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For this reason, it is said that recollection, inference, desire, doubtful cognition, deluded cognition, and so forth—such as [the cognition of] a mirage—are all not direct perception, because they proceed as conceptualizations following what was previously experienced.

Thus, within all conventional existence, cognitions such as those of a jar, number, lifting, existence-ness, and jar-ness are all similar to direct perception; yet they function by constructing other mental images regarding what is substantially real, because they evolve through conceptualization that falsely synthesizes other meanings.
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has already been explained; inference (*anumāna*) shall now be explained.

Regarding the phrase "that which arises from other stated reasons": this refers to knowledge that follows prior knowledge, arising from other established reasons as previously described, and taking that object as its cognitive support.
This is of two kinds:
first, the wisdom that scrutinizes the object of inference, which arises either from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or from inference (*anumāna*);

and second, the recollection that this reason (*hetu*) is inseparable from the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established. By means of this, the force of what was previously stated is accomplished, because one recollects that the reason is necessarily present in similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and so forth.

Because these are the causes for inference regarding both the proximate and the remote, they are both termed "inference" (*anumāna*); this is stated with reference to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).
One should understand that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) likewise cannot be established as a proof (*sādhana*) apart from these.
Therefore, it is said in verse:
A single entity has many properties, Yet their characteristics do not all function together;
Only by distinguishing it from others Is it expressed as being determinately concomitant.
Thus, these characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are also manifold dharmas;
they do not transcend that which is characterized (lakṣya), and it is only these that can indicate it, and nothing else.
The treatise says:
Why is this established as distinct from the aforementioned direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

It is to demonstrate two approaches: here, one should also speak of the result of inference (*anumāna-phala*) as "inference," and there, one should also speak of the cause of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-hetu*) as "direct perception"; neither is precluded.

The means of proof (*sādhana*) and the fallacious means of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) have already been explained; now the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) and the fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) shall be explained.
The verse says:
"Refutation consists of the statement of deficiencies and so forth; fallacious refutation refers to various types [of such statements]."
The Commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "the refutations consisting of omissions and so forth" herein, this refers to the faults of the various members [of a syllogism], such as omissions and the like, previously mentioned.
Each of those individual terms is called a "refutation" (dūṣaṇa), because each one individually demonstrates that the preceding thesis is not well-stated.

Regarding the statement, "What are called 'pseudo-refutations' are various types [of fallacies]," the various pseudo-fallacies that resemble the properties of the thesis and so forth are termed "pseudo-refutations" because they are for the most part established by others to mislead them regarding valid inference (*saddharmānumāna*).

Because it fails to demonstrate the faults of the opponent's position— since it refutes it through irrational means— and because it establishes its own position at the very point where it should be refuted,
it is called a "pseudo-fallacy" (*jāti*) as it belongs to that same category.

If one establishes such a designation within an illogical inference (*anumāna*), or if one fails to recognize the faults of that inference, or even if one intends to reveal the door to those faults, it is not termed a "pseudo-fault" (*jāti*).
The verse says:
Because of the manifestation of different categories;
by establishing through similarity of properties, there is similarity of properties.
The remainder [is established] by way of different dharmas.
"Discrimination" (vikalpa) is so called because it discriminates and distinguishes;
otherwise, there would be only one [entity] without distinction.
To manifest other reasons for what has been established is called "resemblance to obtainability" (*upalabdhisama*).
Because it raises doubts regarding the distinction of meanings, it is termed "hesitation" (*saṃśaya*).
Since it asserts a meaning contrary to the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is undesirable; this is the application of the term's meaning.
The treatise states:
Regarding the phrase here, "Because it demonstrates a different category:

'established by a different same-property' means that because it is established through inversion, it is called 'different establishment'; this is spoken with reference to the instrument and the agent."

"Similarity of the same property" (*sādharmya-sama*) means that which is similar to the same property; it is so named because it is a fallacy of similarity among all the categories established within the *sarvopasaṃhāra* (universal application).
The term "similarity" (*sama*) is a neuter noun, used here because it functions as a refutation of the corresponding argument, or for the sake of conforming to the meter of the verse.
What is the refutation by means of similarity through shared properties?
It is stated thus because [the cause] is spoken of as the "agent" with respect to what is produced, and because it is transmitted as that which brings about origination;
subsequently, it is also stated accordingly in whatever manner is appropriate.
In this context, because it is established through an inverted application of the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), it is called "similarity by similarity" (*sādharmya-sama*).
For example, when one establishes: "Sound is impermanent, because it is produced by volitional effort," and uses space as the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
There are those who take space (*ākāśa*) as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), arguing that because it lacks material form and so forth, "sound is eternal.

In this case, the pot mentioned in the reason (*hetu*) should be the similar instance; yet, instead, space—which belongs to the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)—is asserted as the similar instance. This is therefore called "similarity to the similar instance" (*sādharmya-sama*).

"By another through a different property" means that similarity by a different property (*vaidharmya-samā*) is the counterpart to the aforementioned similarity by the same property (*sādharmya-samā*).

It demonstrates a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), being established through an inverted example of a different property; among the two types of examples, as previously established, a jar is taken as the example of a different property. Therefore, it is called similarity by a different property.

Regarding the statement, "Discriminating distinctions is called discrimination": because the previous [section] explained the manifestation and so forth, while the present [section] explains the discrimination of distinctions, one should understand that discrimination consists of the distinctions among phenomena of the same kind (*sabhāga-dharma*).

That is to say, as previously stated, the jar is taken as the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*); since within that similar instance there exists the distinct property of being combustible and so forth, it follows that the jar must be impermanent;
yet sound is not [combustible], therefore sound must be permanent.

Because there are distinctions such as "incapable of being burned" and so forth, this [position] is established through conceptualization and inversion; therefore, it is called "resemblance to conceptualization.

As for the statement, "It would follow that they become one and there is no difference," this demonstrates that the same fault has already been stated previously, because by virtue of this, [the two] would necessarily become one.
Who is that person?
Because no other expedient means has been heard since then and because they are situated in close proximity, it should be understood that this refers to the [opponent's] own thesis.
"Establishing non-differentiation" means establishing the fallacy of non-differentiation.
Since the meaning can be understood from these very words, there is no need to state whose name it is or with whom it is shared to establish their non-difference.
Because they are not specified separately, "this all" is identical to "that all."

As it has been said: "If one sees that because a jar and other things share common properties (*sādharmya*), they must therefore also lack distinction from other properties, then all properties of a jar would necessarily exist as sound; consequently, all things, being identical in their mutual properties, would become a single nature."

In that case, there would be the fault of establishing no distinction [between the two]; furthermore, it is to demonstrate the difference between the word "vase" and its referent. Since this is not significantly different from the previous analysis of similarity, it should be explained separately.

If one establishes "impermanence" by means of "being produced through uninterrupted effort," with the intent to show that both are non-ultimate natures, then the fallacy of the thesis and the reason being indistinguishable occurs.
Furthermore, because this causes [the subject] to become non-distinct in nature, it is called "non-different similarity" (*aviśeṣasama*).
Some say that this reason, just as it can establish the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), can also establish a property contrary to it.
Because there is no distinction, it is called "similarity through non-difference" (*aviśeṣasama*).

Regarding the statement, "To reveal another reason for that which is to be established is called 'similarity through apprehensibility' (*upalabdhisama*)," this means that if one demonstrates that another reason for the property of the thesis (*sādhyadharma*) can be apprehended, it is then called similarity through apprehensibility.
That is to say, some may argue:

"The proof previously established that 'sound is impermanent' is not a valid reason, because impermanence can be established through other reasons—such as direct perception—in the case of lightning, light, and so forth."
If that [effect] could exist apart from this [cause], then this would not be the cause of that.
Others have proposed a different argument here, claiming that this is not the correct primary cause for the impermanence of that, because it is not pervasive.
As it is said: "The forest possesses deliberation, because it possesses sleep.

Regarding the statement, "Because it is difficult to distinguish the meaning from doubt, it is called *vimarśa* (hesitation)," it is spoken in the feminine gender because it corresponds to a category of logical fallacy (*hetvābhāsa*).
In this context, because the distinction between the meanings of the thesis (*pakṣa*) leads to an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*), it is called the "fallacy of doubt" (*saṃśaya-sama*);
alternatively, because the distinction between the meanings of the reason (*hetu*) leads to uncertainty, it is termed the "fallacy of the class of doubt."
That is to say, some might argue:
"As previously established, 'sound is impermanent because it is produced by volitional effort.
Since we observe that what is produced by volitional effort is either manifested or generated, doubt arises."
Is that which is now established intended to be manifested or to be produced?
Therefore, one should not use such a reason to prove the meaning of impermanence.
Regarding the phrase "Because it expresses the meaning of a dissimilar instance, it is undesirable; name and meaning follow accordingly," this refers to what some say:

If impermanence is defined as that which is produced by diligent effort without interval, then by logical implication, all lightning, light, and so forth that are not produced by diligent effort without interval should necessarily be permanent.
This is called *arthāpatti-sama* (the semblance based on presumptive implication).
One should know that here the latter member of the compound has been omitted; therefore, it is simply termed *vicikitsā* (doubt) and *arthāpatti* (presumptive implication).
Furthermore, for what reason does this *sāmānyadharma-sama* (the semblance based on commonality) differ from the sequence taught by other masters of Hetuvidyā?
Because it resembles the refutation of the "identity" [of the subject], the verse says:
"By virtue of this identity of the property and so forth, it is 'pseudo' because of the many doubts regarding that."
The Commentary states:
The word "many" is used to indicate that there may be other objections, and to reveal what appear to be the fallacies of an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*).

Among these, the first four do not at all correspond to the method of illustration (*dṛṣṭānta-upāya*) as I have explained it. Nevertheless, following worldly conventions of illustration, although they do not explicitly demonstrate that the reason is determinate, they nonetheless encompass its essential nature; therefore, this statement was made.

By employing reasons such as "indeterminate application" (*anaikāntika*) or "equal presence" (*sādhāraṇa*), one establishes one's own position while provisionally asserting that the opponent also possesses this same property; consequently, this results in a fallacy of the "pseudo-indeterminate common" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika-sadṛśa*), or alternatively, it constitutes a "pseudo-contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin-sadṛśa*).
If it is said that [the reason] is intended solely to establish one's own position, how can it be called a "refutation" (dūṣaṇa) when it is "inconclusive" (anaikāntika)?
It is not that this very [reason] is stated as a refutation; rather, by raising the objection that it is inconclusive, it is designated as "inconclusive."
Since the expressed meaning is spoken of within the expressive words, this fault does not arise.
Other instances should likewise be established in this manner.

If the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) one has established suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), or if there is a certainty regarding the reason (*hetu*) such as "being of the same nature" (*tulyadharmatva*) that establishes the point, then that is called a successful refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
Because these [objections] are difficult to refute, if one relies on the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*) cannot negate their nature.

For example, if someone were to establish that "sound is not audible, like a jar," this would be refuted by the fact that sound is directly perceived as being audible; thus, its audibility cannot be used to negate its impermanence, for it is not merely the non-perception [of a property] that can negate it.
If it were otherwise, then even permanence (*nityatva*) would have to be negated.
The second, "non-different similarity," is the fallacy of the pseudo-unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*).
This is because it superimposes arising upon that which was originally non-existent, thereby committing the error of attempting to establish a thesis through a reason that is itself unestablished.
This uses the principle that what was originally non-existent can arise as an ultimate cause to prove non-existence after cessation.
If one were to establish that very point [as a valid proof], it could indeed function as a refutation.

The third [type of fallacy] is the "semblance of similarity" (*aviśeṣa-sama*), which constitutes a pseudo-refutation because it contradicts the thesis being established; it is a semblance because factors such as combustibility are not determinative [of the specific nature of the subject].
If this were definitive, it would constitute a contradiction.
Since a similar instance can be found that renders the thesis indeterminate, it constitutes a fallacy;
if the reason adduced for the thesis also exists in the case of permanence, it can serve as a valid refutation.

Secondly, although [the reason] is not pervasive (*avyāpin*), it does not incur the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*) because there are no other instances [of the reason] apart from those [intended].
If the probandum (*sādhya*) were absent, it could be called a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*); however, in this context, we do not intend to establish that everything is impermanent.

The "resemblance to doubt" (*saṃśaya-sama*) refers to the following: if one attempts to establish the destruction [of the subject] through the uninterrupted exertion of effort, yet adds the production [of the subject] to the probandum to render the reason inconclusive, this is a "pseudo-inconclusive" (*anaikāntika-sama*) fallacy.

If, however, one does not raise a conceptual distinction regarding the probandum, but merely offers an objection by distinguishing the production of the reason itself, this is a "pseudo-unestablished" (*asiddha-sama*) fallacy.
In this context, it is not intended that only arising establishes destruction; rather, both arising and manifestation are subject to destruction, as they are not indeterminate.
By extension, the meaning is similar: since the objection is based on the indeterminacy of inversion, it is a "pseudo-indeterminate" fallacy.

If one were to establish "permanent" and "impermanent" based on whether a thing is produced by uninterrupted effort or not—or if one were to maintain that only what is produced by uninterrupted effort is impermanent and nothing else—then such a position could be subject to refutation.
The verse says:
Whether the cause reaches [the object] or does not reach it, across the three times, it is an unpalatable statement;
whether reaching or not reaching, there is no cause. This is called the fallacy of the deficient reason (*hetv-ābhāsa*).
The treatise states:

"Regarding 'whether the reason reaches [the thesis] or does not reach it, the three times are not acceptable statements; reaching or not reaching constitutes no reason,' this refers to making unacceptable statements regarding whether there is reaching or non-reaching:

if the establishing reason reaches the thesis to be established and thereby establishes it, then because there is no distinction, it would not be the thesis to be established—just as the waters of a pond and the sea merge without difference."
Furthermore, if [the probandum] is not established, it should not be reached by the mark (*liṅga*);
if the thesis (*sādhya*) were established, what would be the reason for this?
If the establishing reason does not reach the thesis, then because there is no distinction between that which does not reach and that which is not a reason, it should fail to be a reason.
This is called the fallacy of the "prior to the probandum" (prāg-asiddha).
Furthermore, one may raise an objection at three points in time:
if the reason (*hetu*) is posited before that which is to be established (*sādhya*), and that which is to be established does not yet exist, then of what is this a reason?
If you say [the cause] exists after [the effect], then that which is to be established is already accomplished; what further need is there for a reason?
If they exist simultaneously, then neither the reason nor that which possesses the reason is established, like the two horns of an ox.
This is called the "pseudo-reason resembling the absence of a cause.
In this context, the difference from the preceding sequence is due to the fact that both are stated as being deficient in a [valid] reason. Why is this so?
This is because it irrationally denies all causes.
What is the reasoning here?
It is simply that they do not reach the same [effect]; therefore, even if they possess the characteristics of a cause, they are not called causes.
What is the reasoning for this?
Because that which exists only prior to the probandum cannot be designated as a "reason" (hetu), it is therefore not a "prover" (sādhana).
Furthermore, in this case, there is the fallacy of self-defeat, as it negates its own [status as a] similar instance (sapakṣa).

Thus, while there are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) regarding the reasons established through words and wisdom, there is a fallacious unestablished reason (*asiddha*) regarding the reasons for the actual meaning, because they irrationally deny the causes of all phenomena.
As with the two preceding reasons, since the established meaning is neither that which is produced nor that which produces, it does not accord with correct reasoning;
if one refutes it by means of correct reasoning, one may be called a "refuter."
The verse says:
Because it asserts that what precedes is causeless, there should be nothing established;
this is termed "resemblance to the non-stated" (*anuktasama*).
The same applies to arising and non-arising.

When the probandum is not established due to a slight difference in the nature of the action, it is called "similarity of the action" (*kāryasama*); this occurs frequently, as in the case of the argument concerning sound.
The treatise states:

"To say that because the preceding reason does not exist, that which is to be established should also not exist, is called 'resemblance to non-statement' (*avācyasama*). This means that some might argue:

"If, as previously established, impermanence is proven by this reason, then since that [reason] did not exist at all prior to its statement, and because the reason is absent, the subject should not be impermanent. Such is termed "resemblance to non-statement."
Regarding the phrase "so too is arising non-arising": since prior to arising there is no cause, there is nothing established.
This is precisely what is called the "fallacy of similarity to non-arising" (*anutpatti-sama*).
As for the word "so too" (*tathāpi*): by analogy with the preceding sound, because the cause does not exist, there should likewise be nothing established.
Now, within this context, just as there is no establishment [of the thesis], one should know that there is also a contradiction to what is established.
That is to say, some say:
"If it is as previously established, then if such a sound did not exist prior to its production through effort and exertion, it would not be impermanent."
Furthermore, because it is not produced by uninterrupted effort, it ought to be eternal.
This is called "resemblance to the unproduced" (*anutpatti-sama*).

Regarding the statement, "When a partial difference in the 'product' (*kṛtaka*) reveals that the thesis is unestablished, it is called 'resemblance to the product' (*kṛtaka-sama*)," this means: if one argues that "sound is impermanent because it is a product, like a jar," then if the jar possesses a different kind of "product-ness" and is thus impermanent, what relevance does that have to the case of sound?
This is called "resemblance to the probandum" (*kāryasama*).

Regarding the phrase "mostly resembling the statement of the thesis," this refers to various forms of resemblance to the stated *sādhya*, such as the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*asiddhahetu*).
The word "often" (*bahuśas*) is used to indicate that [the fallacy] may resemble other types.

In this context, there is no mention of a "similarity-based" (*sādharmya*) *adhyavasita-anumāna* (erroneous inference based on superimposition), namely: establishing impermanence in the words spoken by the proponent because the reason is absent prior to its being stated; this is a case of "apparent non-establishment" (*asiddha-ābhāsa*).
Alternatively, it is an "apparent deficiency of the reason" (*hetv-avaikalya-ābhāsa*), meaning that the capacity to establish [the thesis] is lacking prior to its being stated.

If, within this context, the meaning [of the probandum] is shown to be non-existent, and if at the time of establishing the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) there is no verbal expression, then one may constitute a valid refutation.

Regarding the "fallacy similar to non-arising" (*anutpattisama*): if one imputes the existence of the probandum before the sound has even arisen, and then challenges it on the grounds that the reason (*hetu*) is absent, this is called a "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).
However, if at the time of establishing the proof one demonstrates that this [reason] is non-existent, then one may constitute a valid refutation.

If, prior to its production, one were to challenge [the permanence of sound] by claiming it is not produced through immediate effort (*aprayatnāntarīyaka*), this argument is also seemingly inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it applies by extension to a portion [of the subject].
There are three types of similarity regarding "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*):
if one challenges that being produced—such as in the case of a jar—is absent from sound, this is a fallacy of "apparent non-establishment" (*asiddha*).
If one objects that "being produced" (kṛtakatva) does not exist in jars and the like [as a property of sound], this is a fallacy resembling the contradictory (viruddhābhāsa);
if one objects that it also does not exist in what is eternal (nitya), this is a non-common (asādhāraṇa) reason, and thus it is a fallacy resembling the inconclusive (anaikāntikābhāsa).
Alternatively, this may be considered a fallacy of analogy (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*), because it cites a similar instance (*sādharmya*). Why is this?
It is because inference (*anumāna*) is established by apprehending only the general property (*sāmānya-dharma*), and not by apprehending particularities (*viśeṣa*).
If one were to grasp a distinct meaning based on their definitive difference, then inference would be impossible.
The verse says:
"To seek a reason when both [parties] have already granted [the point] is called the fallacy of 'resemblance to the production of a name'."
This is a challenge raised against the analogy; it is called a "pseudo-analogy.
The treatise states:
"To seek a reason when both [parties] have already granted [the point] is called the 'fallacy of similarity to origination' (utpattisama). This refers to an objection stating:
Regarding the previously established proposition that "jars and the like are impermanent," by what reason is this proven?

As for the statement, "To raise an objection regarding the example is called a 'pseudo-example' (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa)," this means that since both [the proponent and opponent] accept and establish the impermanence of jars and so forth, yet one claims it is not established—thereby raising an objection based on a pseudo-example—it is therefore termed a "pseudo-example."
The verse says:
"Being constantly accompanied by the nature of impermanence, yet being called 'eternally abiding'—
this constitutes the fallacy of establishing a permanent nature, which is described as a fallacy similar to that of the thesis (*pakṣa*)."
The treatise says: There is an objection as follows:

"If it is established as previously stated that 'sound is impermanent,' then this [sound] must be conjoined with both permanence and impermanence, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena never abandons its own essence; therefore, it should also be permanent."
This is what is called the "fallacy of resemblance to permanence" (*nitya-sama*).
It is a fallacy of the thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*) because it superimposes permanence upon that which is established, for there is no such thing as permanent existence.

In this context, there is no separate, real nature of impermanence upon which permanence could depend; rather, it is precisely this intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—being non-existent and now existing, or existing momentarily and then ceasing—that is called "impermanence."
This very state, by virtue of its intrinsic nature and conditions, is termed "impermanence," just as [a fruit] is termed "sourness" and so forth.
Such fallacies are for the most part what Bhadanta Dignāga described as "pseudo-refutations," because they are most widely established as such.
What is explained in other treatises should likewise be established through such differentiation.
These very same types of fallacies, though established as infinite varieties due to slight differences in their specific applications, are not mentioned here for that reason.

In this very context, whatever has been stated regarding superimposition (*samāropa*), denial (*apavāda*), manifestation (*prakāśa*), non-manifestation (*aprakāśa*), the principle of production (*utpatti-nīti*), distinct analogies (*pṛthag-upamāna*), and similarity of categories (*jāti-sādṛśya*)—all of these should be scrutinized and refuted according to this same methodological approach.

Various unwholesome proponents of inference employ such methods of exposition that they proliferate and ramify indefinitely; therefore, as this would lead to an endless discussion beyond the scope of other treatises, it shall not be further elaborated here.

Furthermore, regarding points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), whatever was stated by former masters of logic (*hetuvidyācārya*) has been omitted from this record: some fall within the category of "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*); some are excessively crude; and some are irrational, such as the class of deceptive speech (*kaitavavākya*). Thus, they have not been included here.
All the categories and meanings asserted by other masters should likewise be analyzed and established in this manner.

Such [notions] as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and its divisions are all unreasonable, as they contradict the characteristics already explained; they are all termed "ignorance" because they are extremely remote from the truth.
Furthermore, regarding these types of fallacious expressions, I have already largely refuted them within my own school’s *Tarkaśāstra* and other works.
Moreover, I have already analyzed this point in detail in my critique of the ancient *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*; therefore, let us now desist.
The verse says:
To dispel the poison of ignorance from the wisdom of the learned, I open this gateway of sublime meaning and correct principle.
May all those who are deluded by external measures Transcend the deviant paths and realize the true meaning.
*Hetuvidyānyāyamukhaśāstra*, one fascicle.
